### What it brings together

The notebook connects **modal biodiversity and programmable coupling** with **artificial-life mechanism discovery**, then develops the operational framework: spectra, resolvents, nonlinear response, gauge equivalence, quality-diversity, human feedback, descriptor revision, and strategically communicating scientific agents.

The central proposal is:

> **Discover useful dynamical organizations first, determine which differences actually change their responses, then investigate which physical substrates can implement them.**

Kagome, tensegrity, moiré, spintronics, photonics, and MXenes appear as candidate design domains, rather than interchangeable implementations.

### The calculations are included, not just described

| Demonstration | What the executed example establishes |
|---|---|
| **Gauge-flux triangle** | Two states with identical eigenvalues route signals to opposite labeled outputs at the chosen operating point. |
| **Non-normal dynamics** | Identical eigenvalues can conceal substantially different transient amplification and resolvent gain. |
| **Nonlinear memory** | Systems with the same local derivative can have different global attractor basins and switching possibilities. |
| **Artificial-life repertoire mining** | Exhaustive evaluation of all **256 elementary cellular-automaton rules**, under a specified boundary/input protocol, distinguishes transformation counts from input-preserving behavior. |
| **Descriptor audit** | **384 raw representations** reduce to **24 gauge-invariant flux classes**, while an insufficient measurement protocol still merges distinct states. |

That last example adds an important refinement: **even a response-based archive can miss diversity when its tests are too narrow**. The notebook distinguishes true coordinate equivalence from “these designs look equivalent under the measurements we happened to make.”

### Ready for collaboration, with the evidence boundaries intact

There is a proposal-ready abstract, concrete agent communication protocol, matched-budget benchmark design, human-feedback procedure, and machine-readable claim ledger. The ledger separates **established precedent, executed results, proposed experiments, analogies, and unverified reading leads**.

**Nothing has been publicly posted.** This is a publication-oriented methods and research-proposal notebook with working demonstrations, not a completed study claiming that a swarm or physical device has outperformed existing approaches.

**Yes. Artificial life should be a major source of computational mechanisms for this project, not merely another category of simulated materials.** My earlier framing was too restricted to choosing a lattice and inspecting its modes.

The broader program would be:

\[
\boxed{
\text{generate artificial-life dynamics}
\rightarrow
\text{identify their causal and spectral organization}
\rightarrow
\text{extract useful computational mechanisms}
\rightarrow
\text{find substrates that can reproduce them}.
}
\]

Instead of asking only, “What can Kagome do?”, we would also ask:

> **What interesting forms of memory, routing, selective coupling, recovery, and collective computation already emerge in artificial worlds, and what is the smallest physical system that can implement each one?**

There are surprisingly direct precedents in the communities you named.

## 1. Cross Labs already studied something remarkably close to our “repertoire of transformations”

Martin Biehl and Olaf Witkowski’s paper **“Investigating Transformational Complexity: Counting Functions a Region Induces on Another in Elementary Cellular Automata”** asks how many different transformations a surrounding region can induce on an enclosed region. It connects that question to controllability, physical universality, and constructor theory. citeturn335240view0

The connection to your project is immediate.

Imagine an interior region with state \(x\), surrounded by an environment configured as \(e\). After some specified evolution time:

\[
x\longmapsto f_e(x).
\]

Different surrounding configurations implement different functions:

\[
\mathscr F=\{f_e:e\in\mathcal E\}.
\]

**The surrounding material becomes part of the program.**

That is a discrete, nonlinear cousin of our proposed repertoire

\[
\mathscr R_x=\{H_{\mathrm{IO}}(\omega,\lambda)\},
\]

where controls \(\lambda\) change a material’s input-output response.

The crucial shift is from counting **states that exist** to counting **transformations that can be reliably induced**. The cellular-automaton paper provides a concrete precedent for investigating that distinction, although it does not establish that its transformations transfer directly into electronic or mechanical hardware. citeturn335240view0

For the institutional connection: Cross Labs closed on August 31, 2026; Witkowski’s research direction continues at independent Nooma Labs. Nooma explicitly describes its program around agency, open-ended learning, collective intelligence, and embodiment/computation. citeturn414745search4turn140235view0

**So your Cross Labs/Nooma connection is not just philosophical affinity. There is already relevant mathematics about the diversity of operations that one region can impose on another.**

## 2. Levin’s work suggests mining the dynamics that preserve an organization, not just its appearance

The neural cellular automata work coauthored by Michael Levin trains local update rules that can grow and regenerate patterns. The significant object is not only the final image: it is the distributed dynamics that bring many different damaged or incomplete states back toward that image. citeturn263930search19turn335240view3

For your purposes, we could mine:

\[
\text{perturbation}
\rightarrow
\text{collective response}
\rightarrow
\text{return to a functional state}.
\]

That potentially gives us **error-correcting dynamics, distributed memory, and reconfiguration policies**.

A particularly relevant 2026 preprint by Jesse Cool, Benedikt Hartl, Levin, and Samantha Petti studies Lenia patterns exposed to regions where their interactions are occluded. The authors map spatial sensitivity and interpret the behavior through attractor-basin geometry: the patterns can change heading while preserving their morphology. That is a study of behavioral and dynamical organization, not evidence of a general-purpose intelligent material. citeturn335240view1

The design lesson I would extract is:

> **Some coordinates should be free to change so that other coordinates can remain stable.**

For a computational material, perhaps routing can reorganize while an encoded state persists. Or local oscillator phases can adjust while a collective timing relationship survives. Those are hypotheses to test, not consequences guaranteed by copying a Lenia pattern.

This is a richer target than either “maximize stability” or “maximize diversity”:

\[
\boxed{
\text{stability of function}
+
\text{flexibility of implementation}.
}
\]

## 3. We should mine several different structures, not call everything a spectrum

Here is the research map I would use. The last column contains **candidate uses to test**, not claims that every artificial-life system already performs them.

| Structure to extract | What it distinguishes | Candidate computational role |
|---|---|---|
| **Local Jacobian spectrum** | Fast, slow, growing, decaying, and oscillatory perturbations around a state | Relaxation, filtering, sensitive directions |
| **Floquet modes and phase-response curves** | How a repeating pattern responds at different points in its cycle | Timing, synchronization, phase-gated communication |
| **Resolvent singular vectors and gains** | Which inputs strongly excite which outputs | Selective addressing, routing, amplification |
| **Finite-time response operators** | How perturbations propagate through a changing organism or collective | Transient processing and moving communication channels |
| **Koopman and transfer-operator structure** | Coherent observables, slow transitions, and persistent dynamical organization | Reduced models and long-timescale state tracking |
| **Attractor basins and transition pathways** | Which states are maintained and how switching occurs | Memory, reset, recovery, context switching |
| **Hankel singular values and memory-capacity profiles** | Which internal states are both writable and readable | Useful memory rather than merely persistent activity |
| **Higher-order response functions** | Effects that appear only when inputs interact | Coincidence detection, conditional routing, nonlinear mixing |
| **Local causal states and interaction grammars** | Predictively distinct domains, mobile structures, and their interactions | Distributed symbolic or particle-like computation |
| **Adaptive coupling rules** | How the system changes its own future responses | Stateful routing, self-repair, adaptive coordination |

These are distinct analytical tools. For example, phase/isostable analysis describes perturbations around periodic behavior; residual dynamic mode decomposition addresses reliable Koopman spectral estimation; and local causal-state methods identify coherent structures from their predictive organization. None is a universal substitute for the others. citeturn263930search0turn146871search4turn263930search18

**The object worth archiving is therefore not just an organism or a matrix. It is an organized response mechanism, together with the conditions under which it works.**

## 4. How spectral and resolvent mining would actually work

Suppose an artificial-life simulator has update rule

\[
x_{t+1}=F_\theta(x_t,u_t),
\]

where \(x_t\) contains the full state, \(\theta\) specifies its rules, and \(u_t\) is an intervention we deliberately apply.

We can ask several increasingly rich questions.

### A. What are the local response modes?

Around a reference trajectory:

\[
\delta x_{t+1}
=
A_t\delta x_t+B_t\delta u_t,
\]

with

\[
A_t=\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial x},
\qquad
B_t=\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial u}.
\]

The eigenstructure of \(A_t\) describes local perturbational behavior. But **the state matters**: the same update rule can generate different \(A_t\) at different points in its dynamics.

So we would not store only:

> “This artificial organism has these eigenvalues.”

We would store:

> “In this operating regime, these perturbations decay rapidly, these persist, and these trigger a transition.”

That is the distinction between mining a single spectrum and mining a **state-dependent family of spectra**.

### B. Which modes are actually accessible?

Near a fixed operating point, the discrete-time resolvent is

\[
R(z)=(zI-A)^{-1}.
\]

With input and readout maps \(B,C\),

\[
H(z)=C(zI-A)^{-1}B.
\]

Then

\[
H(z)=U(z)\Sigma(z)V(z)^\dagger
\]

identifies input patterns, corresponding output patterns, and their gains.

For a Lenia-like system, a proposed experiment could ask:

> Which spatial pattern of small stimulation makes a distant region respond, while minimally disturbing the rest of the structure?

The answer might be a spatially extended input rather than a single poke. It might also depend strongly on frequency or operating state.

**This is how “hidden modal diversity” becomes an addressable computational resource.** But high gain alone is not a virtue: we would also test noise sensitivity, response repeatability, and whether the output is distinguishable from background activity.

### C. What if the system never sits still?

A developing, traveling, or reorganizing pattern generally does **not** have one fixed transfer function.

Then we should measure a time-dependent response kernel:

\[
K_{t,s}
=
C_tA_{t-1}\cdots A_{s+1}B_s,
\qquad t>s.
\]

It answers:

> If I perturb the system at time \(s\), what changes at time \(t\)?

This is particularly relevant to your strategically coupled agents. The useful channel might exist only during part of a trajectory.

For periodic behavior, Floquet and phase-response methods provide more appropriate descriptions than treating the system as stationary. They distinguish displacement along a cycle from perturbations away from it, and characterize how timing affects the response. citeturn263930search0turn263930search24

Our search target could therefore include:

\[
\boxed{
\text{channels that are mostly closed}
+
\text{specific temporal windows in which they become effective}.
}
\]

That is a concrete form of rare coupling, rather than merely sparse connectivity.

## 5. Koopman theory is an especially direct bridge, but not a magic compression trick

For an autonomous nonlinear update \(x_{t+1}=F(x_t)\), the Koopman operator acts on observables:

\[
(\mathcal K\psi)(x)=\psi(F(x)).
\]

Instead of following every microscopic variable directly, we study functions of the state: shape, concentration, orientation, collective phase, or other learned observables.

The operator is linear in those observables, even when \(F\) is nonlinear. Koopman-resolvent theory explicitly develops spectral descriptions for nonlinear dynamics, including convergence to equilibria and limit cycles. citeturn146871search1

For your project, we could look for observables that reveal:

- a slow collective memory coordinate;
- several persistent oscillatory organizations;
- weakly interacting dynamical sectors;
- a small set of variables that predicts transitions between regimes.

However, **the exact observable space can be infinite-dimensional**, and a small fitted matrix can produce misleading spectral features. Residual DMD was developed partly to detect spurious modes and handle continuous spectral structure with error control. citeturn146871search4

So the swarm should not accept:

> “The fitted Koopman model has an interesting eigenvalue.”

It should demand:

> “This feature survives changes in data, resolution, observable dictionary, and prediction horizon, and improves predictions of an independently tested response.”

That makes the spectrum a scientific instrument rather than decorative numerology.

## 6. Some of the best structures are not primarily spectral

### Attractor-basin geometry

Two systems can have similar local relaxation rates but respond very differently to a large disturbance. One returns to the same state; another switches into a different state; a third fails entirely.

For each candidate, I would map **recovery regions and switching boundaries**, not merely count attractors.

This connects directly to the targeted-perturbation and basin-geometry analysis in the Levin-associated Lenia preprint. citeturn335240view1

The potential computational primitive is:

> Maintain a state against ordinary disturbances, but switch reliably under a particular structured input.

### Writable and readable memory

A slowly changing internal variable is not automatically useful memory. We need an input to write it and an output to reveal it.

For stable linear models, balancing methods use controllability and observability together; Hankel singular values characterize state directions that matter to input-output behavior. citeturn146871search14

For nonlinear candidates, we can test memory operationally: how well can a fixed readout recover past inputs, combinations of past inputs, or temporal relationships? The information-processing-capacity framework provides a precedent for distinguishing different computational functions supported by a dynamical system. citeturn859694search2

**A highly visible oscillation might carry almost no useful input history. A visually quiet internal state might carry substantial memory.**

### Coherent structures and interaction rules

Another route is to identify persistent traveling structures and determine what happens when they meet.

Rupe and Crutchfield’s local causal-state work discovers domains, coherent structures, and interactions in cellular automata using predictive organization rather than a library of predefined shapes. citeturn263930search18turn263930search22

Our extension would be to test whether such interactions implement reusable functions:

\[
(A,B,\text{relative timing},\text{context})
\longmapsto
C.
\]

These are **emergent computational objects**, not literal electrons or quantum quasiparticles. The possible transfer is their interaction logic, not their visual resemblance to particles.

## 7. Flow-Lenia already points toward mining entire ecologies

Flow-Lenia adds mass conservation and localized parameters that move with the simulated matter, allowing different patterns with different local rules to coexist and interact. That makes it relevant not only to diversity among organisms, but to diversity in **how different dynamical organizations share an environment**. citeturn950042academia35turn950042search30

The paper **“Exploring Flow-Lenia Universes with a Curiosity-driven AI Scientist”** searches system-level behavior using evolutionary-activity, compression, and multiscale-distribution metrics, with an interactive tool for human exploration. It reports broader coverage than random search within its chosen descriptor space. citeturn587872view1

That is close to your human-AI/QD idea already.

Our proposed extension would be to add **intervention-based descriptors**:

\[
\text{which component influences which}
\]

\[
\text{under what context}
\]

\[
\text{with what delay}
\]

\[
\text{while preserving which independent dynamics}.
\]

For example, consider a *hypothetical* discovery:

> Two subsystems maintain separate rhythms. A third, slowly changing state permits phase exchange only after a particular history of stimulation.

A schematic model might be

\[
\dot a=f(a)+g(q)h(a,b),
\]

\[
\dot b=k(b)+g(q)\tilde h(a,b),
\]

\[
\dot q=\varepsilon r(q,a,b,u).
\]

Here \(q\) controls the coupling, and \(\varepsilon\) creates a slower timescale.

**The thing to mine is not just the oscillators. It is the state-dependent rule that decides when they interact.**

That is the same principle you wanted for the scientific swarm: independence by default, integration when a specific condition makes it useful.

## 8. We should distinguish appearance search from response search

ASAL, **“Automating the Search for Artificial Life with Foundation Models,”** uses foundation-model representations to guide searches across renderable artificial-life systems. It provides a useful precedent for searching across different simulation families, rather than hand-designing every interesting result. citeturn263930view0

But for our objective, visual or semantic novelty would be a **discovery heuristic**, not the final score.

We need to distinguish:

\[
\underbrace{\text{different-looking, same function}}_{\text{possibly redundant}}
\]

from

\[
\underbrace{\text{same-looking, different response}}_{\text{possibly important}}.
\]

The gauge/quotient agent now has a broader, carefully defined role. It could check whether apparent novelty is caused by translation, rotation, phase offset, relabeling, or a different internal realization of the same tested behavior.

But those equivalences depend on the task. A translation can be irrelevant when studying free locomotion and crucial when input and output ports are fixed. Nor should we call every removable coordinate a physical gauge symmetry.

The archive should preserve **differences that survive appropriate equivalence tests and predict different intervention outcomes**.

## 9. How the swarm would mine this, concretely

I would add an artificial-life discovery track alongside the lattice track, with six tightly specified roles.

| Agent | Deliverable | When it should communicate |
|---|---|---|
| **World explorer** | Reproducible update rules, seeds, and candidate operating regimes | It finds an unexplored dynamical behavior |
| **Spectral investigator** | Local/Floquet/Koopman features with validity checks | Similar-looking candidates have different dynamical organization |
| **Intervention investigator** | Response kernels, input-output gains, and causal counterexamples | Spectral similarity fails to predict responses |
| **Memory and recovery investigator** | Write/read tests, switching boundaries, and recovery maps | A candidate has a useful history-dependent behavior |
| **Equivalence critic** | Tests for redundant representations and false novelty | The archive may be counting copies as discoveries |
| **Mechanism compiler** | A reduced model and candidate physical implementation | A behavior survives independent validation |

The critical communication event would be something like:

> **“Candidates A and B have similar local spectra, but only B preserves an input after a disturbance. Please identify the smallest dynamical feature that explains the difference.”**

A temporary coalition investigates that discrepancy. It might identify nonlinear basin geometry, a hidden slow variable, or a context-dependent coupling. That finding becomes either a new descriptor or a reason to reject the original spectral explanation.

Humans would compare **responses and mechanisms**, not just animations:

> Does this pair demonstrate a genuinely different way to preserve memory, or merely a different arrangement of the same feedback loop?

Witkowski’s work with Kevin Frans and L. B. Soros on **Selecting for Selection** is also relevant: it investigates learning selection policies that balance diversification and adaptation. It is a precedent for evolving how search selects candidates, not proof that the same policy will work in our domain. citeturn335240view4

## 10. Then comes the hard bridge: compiling dynamics into matter

Suppose the artificial-life track discovers a useful mechanism:

> A transient input writes a persistent state; the state gates later signal propagation; moderate damage does not erase the behavior.

We should not try to reproduce its entire artificial organism in a material.

Instead:

\[
\text{large artificial-life system}
\rightarrow
\text{minimal validated dynamical model}
\rightarrow
\text{candidate implementation}.
\]

The reduced model might require only a few state variables, nonlinear feedback, and a controllable coupling. We could then ask whether a proposed electronic, magnetic, mechanical, photonic, or hybrid system can implement those requirements.

**The transfer criterion should be agreement on interventions, not just agreement on eigenvalues.**

For a chosen input family \(\mathcal U\), a proposed objective is

\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{transfer}}
=
\mathbb E_{u\sim\mathcal U}
\left[
\|y_{\mathrm{ALife}}[u]-y_{\mathrm{target}}[u]\|^2
\right],
\]

supplemented by tests of switching, recovery, noise tolerance, and operating cost.

Several constraints must remain explicit. A simulated rule might require nonlocal information, external energy, asymmetric coupling, or fast parameter changes. An implementation must supply those resources rather than silently assuming them away.

And **an artificial-life simulator running on a GPU has not demonstrated a hardware advantage**. It has supplied a candidate mechanism. Any speed, energy, or robustness advantage still needs an end-to-end comparison including control and readout.

There is even a relevant interface precedent in the Levin/Witkowski collaboration: the Xenobot-culture study uses motion-derived sonification and acoustic signals to couple biological systems. It is a proof-of-principle biohybrid interface, not an established general communication architecture, but it reinforces the importance of explicitly designing how one dynamical system can affect another. citeturn140235view0turn414745search23

## 11. Can we calculate these structures without DFT?

**For a specified artificial-life model, most of this is numerical analysis of its update rules and trajectories. DFT is not the entry ticket.**

With executable rules, we can calculate derivatives where they exist, run controlled perturbations, estimate response kernels, test recurrence, and fit reduced models. For large states, we would use matrix-free directional derivatives and selected response channels rather than constructing every entry of an enormous Jacobian.

With only videos or observational recordings, we can estimate some dynamical structure, but hidden states and unknown inputs create ambiguity. That is why the proposed workflow needs interventions and held-out prediction tests. Data-driven spectral methods themselves require verification against spurious modes. citeturn146871search4

DFT, calibrated mechanics, magnetic simulation, or experimental characterization enter when we ask:

> **Can this particular real substrate implement the mechanism accurately enough?**

They do not have to precede discovery of the mechanism.

## The strongest version of your project

I would expand the Computational Matter Zoo into **an atlas of transferable dynamical mechanisms**.

The search would preserve diversity in spectra, response channels, memory, recovery, nonlinear interactions, and adaptive coupling. Artificial life supplies candidate organizations; spectral and control theory help characterize them; the swarm finds counterexamples and missing descriptors; materials modeling tests whether the mechanisms can be instantiated elsewhere.

The central hypothesis becomes:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Artificial life can generate useful computational organizations}
\atop
\text{that we would not think to specify directly as a materials-design objective.}
}
\]

**That is a much stronger bridge between Levin, Nooma, and Buehler than “life-inspired materials.” It is: discover how artificial systems organize computation, determine which parts of that organization actually matter, and turn those parts into design targets for matter.**

## But DFT and Thermo-Calc aren't the same obstacle

This is where your point about vibe coding becomes important.

**DFT is principally an algorithmic and computational challenge.** We can write the equations, discretize them, implement self-consistent solvers, and run calculations. Indeed, <Link url="https://www.quantum-espresso.org/" title="Quantum ESPRESSO"/> is already an open-source production DFT suite. Its capabilities include electronic structure, phonons, and several specialized properties. <Cite refs={["turn856360search3","turn856360search8"]}/>

Building a simplified DFT solver is feasible. Rebuilding a production-quality one with reliable pseudopotentials, spin-orbit physics, convergence control, and broad materials support is a much bigger undertaking.

**Thermo-Calc has a different moat: curated thermodynamic knowledge.**

Open-source <Link url="https://pycalphad.org/" title="pycalphad"/> can calculate phase equilibria from thermodynamic databases. But those databases contain experimentally and computationally assessed Gibbs-energy models. Writing an equilibrium solver doesn't conjure up accurate thermodynamic parameters for an uncharacterized alloy. Commercial encrypted databases also aren't automatically readable by pycalphad. <Cite ref="turn856360search2"/>

Likewise, <Link url="https://phonopy.github.io/phonopy/" title="Phonopy"/> can derive phonon dispersions and other quantities from force constants, but those force constants must come from a physical model, another calculation, or measurements. <Cite refs={["turn856360search0","turn856360search4"]}/>

So I would distinguish three things:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Algorithms}
\neq
\text{physical parameters}
\neq
\text{validated predictions}.
}
\]

Vibe coding can dramatically reduce the cost of creating algorithms, interfaces, and automated workflows.

It cannot automatically eliminate the cost of obtaining reliable physical parameters or testing predictions against reality.

## What this means for the agent swarm

I would make the swarm **calculator-independent**, not calculator-free.

The Gauge Agent should be able to compute Wilson loops itself. The Spectral Agent should diagonalize Hamiltonians itself. The Resolvent Agent should solve linear systems itself. These do not require remotely hosted scientific SaaS.

But the swarm should also know when it has reached an inference boundary:

> “I discovered a Kagome configuration with highly selective modal coupling under the assumed hopping parameters. I now need material-specific force constants or electronic hopping estimates to determine whether this behavior survives in a realizable substrate.”

That request could be passed to an open-source DFT solver, a trained interatomic potential, or eventually an experimental collaborator.

The crucial design principle is **a fidelity ladder**:

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <list marker="number" connector="solid" gap={2}>
    <list-item>
      **Analytical and tight-binding physics**

      Extremely cheap exploration of geometry, topology, phases, normal modes and transfer functions.
    </list-item>
    <list-item>
      **Numerical model refinement**

      Larger lattices, nonlinear couplings, disorder, dynamics, realistic boundaries, and uncertainty testing.
    </list-item>

Now suppose we change every site's local phase reference:

\[
|i\rangle\rightarrow e^{i\theta_i}|i\rangle.

The hopping phase changes according to

\[
\phi'_{ij}=\phi_{ij}+\theta_i-\theta_j.

Individual edge phases have changed, but this can be a mere change of basis.

The Gauge Agent checks what survives these transformations.

Around a closed loop:

\[
\boxed{
W_\gamma=
\prod_{(ij)\in\gamma}e^{i\phi_{ij}}
=e^{i\Phi_\gamma}.
}
\]

The local phase changes cancel, so \(W_\gamma\) is gauge-invariant.

This distinction between gauge-dependent hopping phases and invariant Wilson-loop fluxes is standard in lattice gauge descriptions. <Cite ref="turn259441search14" />

## 2. It should search a much smaller, physically meaningful space

A connected graph with \(V\) vertices and \(E\) edges has

\[
\boxed{E-V+1}
\]

independent graph cycles.

For our illustrative 40-site, 75-edge network:

\[
75-40+1=36.
\]

So although there are 75 edge phases, only 36 independent loop-phase coordinates remain after quotienting by local U(1) phase transformations.

The Gauge Agent can do this mechanically:

1. Construct a spanning tree.
2. Use gauge freedom to set phases on its tree edges to zero.
3. Identify the remaining edges, each of which closes an independent cycle.
4. Represent the candidate by those cycle fluxes.

This is a very concrete form of the quotienting idea from the recurrent-reasoning paper you discussed.

The crucial advantage is that the optimizer stops wasting evaluations exploring different parameterizations of the same Hamiltonian.

For spin/valley systems with matrix-valued links, the extension is non-Abelian: ordered Wilson-loop products transform by conjugation, so their traces or eigenvalues can serve as invariant descriptors.

## 1. What the linked paper actually contributes

The paper is **“Looped Reasoning Finishes Earlier Than You Think,” by Sumin Park and T. Konstantin Rusch**. It introduces the **Quotient Recurrent Reasoner, QRR**.

It studies oscillations that can delay recurrent reasoning, while recognizing that indiscriminately suppressing oscillations can damage reasoning. QRR builds in per-token phase symmetry and an invariant readout, then measures convergence modulo that symmetry. Its experiments concern Sudoku, mazes, and Mini-ARC, not materials or agent swarms. citeturn598497view0

Here is the general mathematical principle, independent of any particular neural architecture.

Suppose several states are equivalent under a transformation group:

\[
z\sim g\cdot z.
\]

They belong to the same equivalence class:

\[
[z]=\{g\cdot z:g\in G\}.
\]

If the update respects that equivalence and the output ignores it, then the system can keep changing coordinates while having already finished the relevant computation.

For example, consider an illustrative state

\[
z_t=e^{i\theta_t}v.
\]

Its phase keeps rotating, so \(z_{t+1}\neq z_t\). But an output depending only on \(vv^\dagger\) remains unchanged:

\[
z_tz_t^\dagger=vv^\dagger.
\]

**Motion in the representation is not necessarily progress in the computation.**

For our materials project, that suggests a correction to the earlier emphasis on modal biodiversity:

## 2. The biggest subtlety: three different meanings of “loop”

Your collaborator mentions nonlinear attention represented by loops. That could be a valuable direction, but these three things need separate names:

| Meaning of “loop” | What closes? | What it can tell us |
|---|---|---|
| **Recurrent computation** | A processing block is applied repeatedly | Whether more iterations improve the answer |
| **An oscillatory trajectory** | The state revisits a region of state space | Whether the dynamics rotate, cycle, or approach an attractor |
| **A relational or transport loop** | A path through connected entities returns to its starting point | Whether composed relationships contain information that cannot be removed by changing local coordinates |

A recurrent model can have an oscillatory trajectory without implementing an interesting transport loop. Conversely, a lattice can have meaningful loop-dependent interference while obeying entirely **linear** evolution equations.

That distinction matters directly to the proposed connection.

Also, **linear attention is not synonymous with sparse attention or a linear input-output function**. In the original linear-attention formulation, the central efficiency gain comes from factorizing and reassociating computations to obtain linear complexity in sequence length. The implied token interactions need not be sparse. citeturn216408view0

QRR itself uses **softmax attention**, rather than establishing a linear-attention-plus-loop decomposition. citeturn819289view2

So I would interpret your collaborator as proposing an **extension or complementary architecture**, not simply restating the linked paper.

## Andrea Liu is almost the bridge between Anderson and this idea

Three strands of her work line up remarkably well.

First, **jamming**. Near the jamming transition, disordered packings acquire an excess of low-frequency vibrational modes. Crucially, these aren't just ordinary crystal phonons. Near marginal jamming, the lowest modes can be neither ordinary plane waves nor simply localized vibrations. citeturn187308search2turn187308search7

Second, Liu and collaborators showed that low-frequency quasi-localized modes identify **soft spots**, regions likely to undergo rearrangements. So the vibrational spectrum isn't merely describing the material. Certain modes encode *where and how it can transform*. citeturn187308search1

Third, her allostery work is almost your “tiny impurity changes global computation” idea in engineered-network form. That's striking:

\[
\text{tiny structural intervention}
\rightarrow
\text{huge change in collective response}.

The substrate is effectively being **programmed through its spectrum**.

Carbon doesn't strengthen iron because “more vibrational modes are good.”

\boxed{
\text{small controlled violation of symmetry}

\text{new collective response}

Ordinary message passing assumes that if agent \(i\) sends vector \(x\) to agent \(j\), \(x\) somehow means the same thing on both ends.
